'''Jüri Kukk''' (May 1, 1940 – March 27, 1981) was an [[Estonia]]n [[professor]] of [[chemistry]], anti-Soviet [[dissident]] and political prisoner,<ref name=ret/><ref>[[Rein Taagepera]], [https://www.amazon.com/Softening-without-Liberalization-Soviet-Union/dp/0819138010 ''Softening without Liberalization in the Soviet Union: The Case of Juri Kukk''], 1984, {{ISBN|0-8191-3801-0}}, 254 pp.</ref> who died in the former [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] [[labor camp]] at [[Vologda]].{{#tag:ref|''The New York Times'' incorrectly gave the place of death as [[Murmansk]], repeated in some other sources. [http://oasis.lib.harvard.edu/oasis/deliver/~hou01537 Catalog of photos] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150404020914/http://oasis.lib.harvard.edu/oasis/deliver/~hou01537 |date=2015-04-04 }}, among which some of the grave of Jüri Kukk, one of them titled as "Jüri Kukk's grave site in Vologda Identified by a post bearing his prison number 23781. 30 March 1981"|group=Note}}

Kukk, who initially studied and later taught at the [[University of Tartu]] from 1958 to 1979, was the author of a number of scientific papers. Although he was a member of the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union]], it was apparently Kukk's period of scientific work in France in 1975–1976 that opened his eyes to the severity of the problems in his occupied homeland of Estonia and in the former Soviet Union more broadly. Kukk protested the invasion of Afghanistan by the USSR in 1979, and applied for permission to [[emigrate]] to the West. After being fired by the University of Tartu, he was arrested by the Soviet authorities in February 1980, along with fellow human rights activist [[Mart-Olav Niklus]],<ref name="Seeger">{{cite news |last1=Seeger |first1=Murray |title=Nationalism Underlies Estonian's Death |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-oregonian-jri-kukk-1940-1981/161734617/ |work=The Oregonian |date=May 26, 1981 |location=Portland, OR |page=15 |access-date=December 28, 2024 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> and charged with distribution of "anti-Soviet propaganda".<ref name="Seeger"/> Niklus and Kukk both actively campaigned for Estonia being given the chance to go her way again as an independent nation, free of Soviet domination. Kukk resigned from the Communist Party in 1978<ref name="Seeger"/> and was subsequently fired from the position of associate professor of chemistry at Tartu University. He was also refused permission to emigrate.<ref name=ret>[[Rein Taagepera]], "Estonia: Return to Independence", [https://books.google.com/books?id=8hwE-039tAMC&pg=PA113&dq=%22juri+Kukk%22 pp. 113–115].</ref>

Jüri Kukk was sentenced in January 1980 on charges of "anti-Soviet agitation"<ref name="Seeger"/><ref name="Asbury">{{cite news |title=Estonians Protest Death of Dissident |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/asbury-park-press-jri-kukk-1941-1981/137110050/ |work=Asbury Park Press |date=April 1, 1981 |location=Asbury Park, NJ |page=26 |access-date=December 20, 2023 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> or arrested in February 1980 for contact with foreign correspondents<ref>{{cite news |last1=Foy |first1=Fred |title=Estonian-Americans Supporting Olympic Boycott |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/asbury-park-press-jri-kukk-1940-1981/169092642/ |work=Asbury Park Press |date=April 25, 1980 |location=Asbury Park, NJ |page=C4 |access-date=March 29, 2025 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> and  "distribution of [[anti-Soviet]] [[propaganda]]."<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1981/03/29/world/around-the-world-estonian-dissident-40-said-to-die-in-soviet-camp.html "Around the World; Estonian Dissident, 40, Said to Die in Soviet Camp"].</ref> He started a hunger strike to protest the arrest of fellow dissident [[Mart-Olav Niklus]].<ref name="Asbury"/> Kukk was transported to Vologda on March 24, 1981, where he was tortured and died three days later.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Niklus |first1=Mart |author1-link=Mart-Olav Niklus |title=An Estonian Reports on Life in a Soviet Prison |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-philadelphia-inquirer-jri-kukk-194/136958914/ |work=The Philadelphia Inquirer |date=February 13, 1988 |location=Philadelphia, PA |page=9 |access-date=December 17, 2023 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Kukk had a wife, Silvi, with whom he had two children.<ref name="Asbury"/>
